\chapter{Parting Words}
\label{ch:russian-parting-words}
\hlchaptermodality{11}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can close a Russian conversation with the parting word that fits how long until I see the person again, and say good night.}

The chapter closes on \ru{спокойной} \ru{ночи}, the last word of the day and the surest cognate in the chapter: the reader produces all six parting words in order, names \ru{ночь} and \ru{покой}'s English cousins, and hears the \ru{до} + genitive pattern that links five of the six. It is the first realization of SPINE-TAKE-LEAVE in this track, closing all six of the node's concepts, and it reaches back to Chapter 6 to rescue \ru{ф}, \ru{х}, \ru{чай}, \ru{хлеб} and the request pattern, nothing had revisited since.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[da svidániya]{\ru{до} \ru{свидания} — \textquotedblleft{}goodbye,\textquotedblright{} built on a verb you already own}

\label{lesson:RU-C11-do-svidaniya}



\begin{quote}
Plenty of meeting, greeting and naming so far, and not one word yet for closing the door behind you. That changes now — with a phrase built from a verb you already own.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — \ru{до} \ru{свидания}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ru{до} \ru{свидания}} — \emph{da svidániya} — \textbf{goodbye} (the ordinary, all-purpose parting word)
\end{quote}

Two words, said fast as one: \emph{da-svi-DA-ni-ya}. Every letter is one you already read.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: \ru{до} asks for the genitive}]
\textbf{\ru{до}} means \textquotedblleft{}until,\textquotedblright{} and it always reshapes the word after it — the \textbf{genitive} case, Russian's way of marking \textquotedblleft{}of\textquotedblright{} or \textquotedblleft{}belonging to this event.\textquotedblright{} \emph{\ru{Свидания}} is \emph{\ru{свидание}} wearing the shape \emph{\ru{до}} requires. You do not need the rule behind that shape yet — only that \emph{\ru{до}} always asks for one, and every parting word this chapter teaches will show it again.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ru{свидание}} means \textquotedblleft{}a meeting, a seeing of one another\textquotedblright{} — a noun built on \textbf{\ru{видеться}}, \textquotedblleft{}to see each other,\textquotedblright{} which is your own verb \textbf{\ru{видеть}}, \textquotedblleft{}to see,\textquotedblright{} wearing the reflexive ending and the prefix \textbf{\ru{с}-}, \textquotedblleft{}together.\textquotedblright{} Taken apart, the whole phrase reads: \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}until {[}we{]} see each other again.\textquotedblright{}}

That is not a Russian oddity. \textbf{French \emph{au revoir}} and \textbf{German \emph{auf Wiedersehen}} are built the same way, on their own \textquotedblleft{}see\textquotedblright{} verbs — every one of them says goodbye by promising to look at you again, rather than by naming an ending. Russian's \emph{\ru{видеть}} is the same root you met wearing English clothes as \textbf{wit}, \textbf{wise} and \textbf{video}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\ru{до} \ru{свидания}\textquotedblright{} — \emph{da-svi-DA-ni-ya}, all-purpose goodbye
  \item the verb inside it — \textquotedblleft{}\ru{видеть}, \ru{видеться}, \ru{свидание} — see, see each other, a seeing\textquotedblright{}
  \item the pattern — \textquotedblleft{}\ru{до} + genitive, every time\textquotedblright{}
  \item the three languages — \textquotedblleft{}\ru{до} \ru{свидания}, au revoir, auf Wiedersehen — all 'until the re-seeing'\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}goodbye,\textquotedblright{} the all-purpose way. (\textbf{\ru{До} \ru{свидания}}.) Which familiar verb is hiding inside it, and what does the whole phrase literally mean? (\textbf{\ru{Видеть}}, \textquotedblleft{}to see\textquotedblright{} — literally \textquotedblleft{}until {[}we{]} see each other again.\textquotedblright{}) What case does \textbf{\ru{до}} always ask for? (\textbf{The genitive.}) Name one other language that says goodbye the same way. (\textbf{French \emph{au revoir}} or \textbf{German \emph{auf Wiedersehen}}.) One last look back: what word closed the previous lesson, and what English words share its root? (\textbf{\ru{Сердце}}, \textquotedblleft{}heart\textquotedblright{} — cousin of \emph{heart}, Latin \emph{cor/cordis}, Greek \emph{kardía}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[paká]{\ru{пока} — \textquotedblleft{}bye,\textquotedblright{} the casual half of yesterday's word}

\label{lesson:RU-C11-poka}



\begin{quote}
Every formal word in this book has an informal twin somewhere. Here is \emph{\ru{до} \ru{свидания}}'s — and it turns out to share a root with a word you already own, from the other end of the book entirely.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — \ru{пока}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ru{пока}} — \emph{paká} — \textbf{bye} (casual — friends, family, anyone you'd use \emph{\ru{ты}} with)
\end{quote}

Two syllables, stress on the second: \emph{pa-KÁ}. Reach for \emph{\ru{до} \ru{свидания}} with a stranger or someone older; reach for \emph{\ru{пока}} with exactly the people \emph{\ru{друг}} was about.

\emph{(Note: no genitive here at all — this word does not follow yesterday's \ru{до}-pattern. It is not built the same way, which is your first clue that it has a different history.)}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ru{пока}} is built from \textbf{\ru{по}-} plus an old Slavic pronoun, \textbf{\ru{кыи}}, \textquotedblleft{}which, what kind\textquotedblright{} — the ancestor of the modern word \textbf{\ru{какой}}, \textquotedblleft{}which one.\textquotedblright{} That pronoun descends from the same ancient Indo-European question-root, PIE \textbf{*k\textsuperscript{w}os}, \textquotedblleft{}who,\textquotedblright{} that gives Russian \textbf{\ru{как}} (\textquotedblleft{}how,\textquotedblright{} the question word from \emph{\ru{как} \ru{вас} \ru{зовут}?}) and, on the Germanic branch, the \textbf{entire English wh- family}: \emph{who, what, when, where, why, which}. \textbf{\ru{Пока}} is, at its root, a fossil of \textquotedblleft{}however long\textquotedblright{} or \textquotedblleft{}for the while that\textquotedblright{} — the same idea as English \emph{while}, which shortens \emph{for a while} into \emph{bye for now}.

But the word you are learning to say \textquotedblleft{}bye\textquotedblright{} with is much younger than its root. Dictionaries record \emph{\ru{пока}} as a parting word only from the early 20th century — colloquial slang at first, likely modeled on English \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}so long\textquotedblright{}} — centuries after \emph{\ru{кыи}} had already worn down into \emph{\ru{как}} and \emph{\ru{какой}}. The root is ancient; the goodbye is recent.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\ru{пока}\textquotedblright{} — \emph{pa-KÁ}, casual bye
  \item the pair — \textquotedblleft{}\ru{до} \ru{свидания} for a stranger, \ru{пока} for a \ru{друг}\textquotedblright{}
  \item the root — \textquotedblleft{}\ru{как}, \ru{какой}, \ru{пока} — one ancient question-stem\textquotedblright{}
  \item the timeline — \textquotedblleft{}the root is ancient; the goodbye is 20th century\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}bye,\textquotedblright{} casually. (\textbf{\ru{Пока}}.) Which two earlier words share its root, and what English word-family is their cousin? (\textbf{\ru{Как}} and \textbf{\ru{какой}}; English \emph{who, what, when, where, why, which}.) Does \emph{\ru{пока}} follow yesterday's \emph{\ru{до}} + genitive pattern? (\textbf{No} — it is built differently.) How old is \emph{\ru{пока}}'s use as a farewell? (\textbf{Only since the early 20th century.}) One more look back: what word closes on the letter \textbf{\ru{ц}}, and what does that letter say? (\textbf{\ru{Сердце}}; \textbf{\ru{ц}} says \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}ts.\textquotedblright{}})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[da skórava]{\ru{до} \ru{скорого} — \textquotedblleft{}see you soon,\textquotedblright{} and a root that goes nowhere in English}

\label{lesson:RU-C11-do-skorogo}



\begin{quote}
Back to yesterday's \emph{\ru{до}} + genitive pattern — and to a word whose trail, unlike \emph{\ru{свидания}}'s, simply stops before it reaches English.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — \ru{до} \ru{скорого}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ru{до} \ru{скорого}} — \emph{da skórava} — \textbf{see you soon}
\end{quote}

Same shape as \emph{\ru{до} \ru{свидания}}: \textbf{\ru{до}} plus a genitive. The word underneath is \textbf{\ru{скорый}}, \textquotedblleft{}quick\textquotedblright{} or \textquotedblleft{}soon\textquotedblright{} — so this is literally \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}until the soon {[}thing/meeting{]}.\textquotedblright{}} Say it \emph{da-SKÓ-ra-va}; that final \textbf{-\ru{ого}} is spelled with a \textbf{\ru{г}} but said like a \textbf{\ru{в}}, a small spelling-versus-sound gap that shows up on this exact ending across the whole language, not just here.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ru{скорый}} is native Slavic, from a Proto-Indo-European root reconstructed as \textbf{*sker-}, \textquotedblleft{}to jump, to hurry\textquotedblright{} — the same root, on the Baltic branch, as Lithuanian \emph{skėrỹs}, \textquotedblleft{}locust\textquotedblright{} (a jumping insect, and a vivid enough image for \textquotedblleft{}quick\textquotedblright{} that it needs no further gloss). Slavic languages keep a whole family on this root: Russian \textbf{\ru{скоро}} (\textquotedblleft{}soon\textquotedblright{}), Ukrainian \textbf{\ru{скорий}}, Polish \textbf{skory}, Bulgarian \textbf{\ru{скоро}}.

Unlike yesterday's \emph{\ru{до} \ru{свидания}}, this root \textbf{does not reach English at all} — no confident cousin, on any branch. That is a different kind of honesty than \emph{\ru{пока}}'s: \emph{\ru{пока}} had an ancient root but a young use as a farewell; \emph{\ru{скорый}} has an ancient root and an ancient use, and simply never left a descendant in the language you already speak. \emph{\ru{Читать}} and \emph{\ru{рот}} taught you this shape of sentence already — some roots travel to England, and some do not, and a good etymology says so either way.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\ru{до} \ru{скорого}\textquotedblright{} — \emph{da-SKÓ-ra-va}, see you soon
  \item the shape — \textquotedblleft{}\ru{до} + genitive, like \ru{до} \ru{свидания}\textquotedblright{}
  \item the honest gap — \textquotedblleft{}\emph{sker-}, 'to hurry' — no English cousin at all\textquotedblright{}
  \item the \ru{г}-as-\ru{в} spelling — \textquotedblleft{}-\ru{ого}, said -ova\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}see you soon.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{\ru{До} \ru{скорого}}.) What word for \textquotedblleft{}quick, soon\textquotedblright{} is it built from, in the genitive? (\textbf{\ru{Скорый}.}) Does it have a secure English cousin? (\textbf{No} — PIE \emph{*sker-}, \textquotedblleft{}to hurry,\textquotedblright{} with no confident descendant in English.) What grammatical pattern does it share with \emph{\ru{до} \ru{свидания}}? (\textbf{\ru{До} + genitive.}) One more look back: what does the letter \textbf{\ru{ц}} say, and which word taught it to you? (\textbf{\textquotedblleft{}Ts,\textquotedblright{} as in \emph{cats}}; from \textbf{\ru{сердце}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[da záftra]{\ru{до} \ru{завтра} — \textquotedblleft{}see you tomorrow,\textquotedblright{} with the dawn hiding inside it}

\label{lesson:RU-C11-do-zavtra}



\begin{quote}
A precise version of \textquotedblleft{}see you soon\textquotedblright{} — more definite than \emph{\ru{до} \ru{скорого}}, warmer than \emph{\ru{пока}} — and, taken apart, a word for \textquotedblleft{}tomorrow\textquotedblright{} that turns out to be built directly on the word for \textquotedblleft{}morning.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — \ru{до} \ru{завтра}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ru{до} \ru{завтра}} — \emph{da záftra} — \textbf{see you tomorrow}
\end{quote}

Unlike the last two lessons, \textbf{\ru{завтра}} does not change shape after \textbf{\ru{до}} — it is an adverb, not a noun, so it has no genitive to show. Say it \emph{da-ZÁF-tra}, with the \textbf{\ru{в}} devoicing to an \emph{f} sound in front of the voiceless \textbf{\ru{т}} that follows it — the same kind of small sound-shift you already handle in \emph{\ru{здравствуйте}}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ru{завтра}} splits cleanly into \textbf{\ru{за}-}, \textquotedblleft{}beyond, after,\textquotedblright{} and \textbf{\ru{утро}}, \textquotedblleft{}morning\textquotedblright{} — so \textquotedblleft{}tomorrow\textquotedblright{} is literally \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}after-the-morning.\textquotedblright{}} And \emph{\ru{утро}} is not a dead end the way last lesson's \emph{\ru{скорый}} was: it continues Proto-Indo-European \textbf{*h\textsubscript{2}ews-}, \textquotedblleft{}to shine, to dawn\textquotedblright{} — the very root behind English \textbf{east} (the direction dawn comes from), Latin \textbf{aurora} (\textquotedblleft{}dawn,\textquotedblright{} and the name of the Roman dawn-goddess), and Greek \textbf{ēōs} (\textquotedblleft{}dawn,\textquotedblright{} also a goddess's name). Say \emph{\ru{утро}}, \emph{east}, \emph{aurora}, \emph{ēōs} in a row and you are tracing one ancient sunrise across four languages.

So \emph{\ru{до} \ru{скорого}} and \emph{\ru{до} \ru{завтра}} make a matched pair: one word this book could not connect to English at all, and the very next one buried inside a word you use to talk about breakfast — the kind of contrast that only shows up when you keep asking the question honestly, lesson after lesson.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\ru{до} \ru{завтра}\textquotedblright{} — \emph{da-ZÁF-tra}, see you tomorrow
  \item the split — \textquotedblleft{}\ru{за}- 'after' + \ru{утро} 'morning'\textquotedblright{}
  \item the cousins — \textquotedblleft{}\ru{утро}, east, aurora, ēōs — one root, four languages\textquotedblright{}
  \item the contrast — \textquotedblleft{}\ru{скорого} had no cousin; \ru{завтра} has three\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}see you tomorrow.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{\ru{До} \ru{завтра}}.) Split it into its two parts and give their meanings. (\textbf{\ru{За}-}, \textquotedblleft{}after\textquotedblright{} + \textbf{\ru{утро}}, \textquotedblleft{}morning.\textquotedblright{}) Name three English/Latin/Greek cousins of \emph{\ru{утро}}. (\textbf{East, aurora, ēōs.}) Does \emph{\ru{завтра}} take a genitive after \emph{\ru{до}}, the way \emph{\ru{скорого}} did? (\textbf{No} — it is an adverb, unchanged.) One quick look back: what is the word for \textquotedblleft{}eye,\textquotedblright{} and what did it originally mean as slang? (\textbf{\ru{Глаз}} — \textquotedblleft{}round stone.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[da fstréchi]{\ru{до} \ru{встречи} — \textquotedblleft{}see you later,\textquotedblright{} a meeting built from two prefixes}

\label{lesson:RU-C11-do-vstrechi}



\begin{quote}
Vaguer than \emph{\ru{до} \ru{завтра}}, warmer than \emph{\ru{до} \ru{скорого}} — the fifth parting word, and the last one built on the \emph{\ru{до}} + genitive pattern.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — \ru{до} \ru{встречи}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ru{до} \ru{встречи}} — \emph{da fstréchi} — \textbf{see you later} (no specific time promised, unlike \emph{\ru{завтра}})
\end{quote}

\emph{\ru{До}} plus the genitive of \textbf{\ru{встреча}}, \textquotedblleft{}a meeting\textquotedblright{} — the fourth phrase in a row to follow that shape. Say it \emph{da-FSTRÉ-chi}: four consonants in a row at the front (\textbf{\ru{в}-\ru{с}-\ru{т}-\ru{р}-}), which is genuinely a mouthful even for a native speaker, so slow down on the approach and let each one land.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ru{встреча}} takes apart by its pieces rather than by a single ancient root: \textbf{\ru{в}-}, \textquotedblleft{}into,\textquotedblright{} plus \textbf{\ru{с}-}, \textquotedblleft{}with, together,\textquotedblright{} on an old Slavic base meaning roughly \textquotedblleft{}to come upon.\textquotedblright{} Put together, it is close to what English \emph{meet} does when it means \textquotedblleft{}to come together\textquotedblright{} — but that closeness is a match of \textbf{idea}, not of \textbf{ancestry}: there is no secure shared root behind the two words, the same honest gap this chapter already met in \emph{\ru{скорого}}.

That makes two of this chapter's five words so far with \textbf{no} confirmed English cousin (\emph{\ru{скорого}}, \emph{\ru{встречи}}), against three that connect cleanly (\emph{\ru{свидания}}, \emph{\ru{пока}}'s root, \emph{\ru{завтра}}). A chapter of goodbyes turns out to be as good a place as any to see that ratio plainly: a good deal of what a language says every day traces back to something you already know, and a good deal simply does not, and neither half is the \textquotedblleft{}real\textquotedblright{} Russian.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\ru{до} \ru{встречи}\textquotedblright{} — \emph{da-FSTRÉ-chi}, see you later
  \item the pieces — \textquotedblleft{}\ru{в}- 'into' + \ru{с}- 'with' + an old 'come upon' root\textquotedblright{}
  \item idea vs. ancestry — \textquotedblleft{}close to \emph{meet} in meaning, not in history\textquotedblright{}
  \item the running count — \textquotedblleft{}\ru{два} \ru{из} \ru{пяти} \ru{без} \ru{английского} \ru{кузена} so far\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}see you later.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{\ru{До} \ru{встречи}}.) Which two prefixes is \emph{\ru{встреча}} built from? (\textbf{\ru{В}-}, \textquotedblleft{}into,\textquotedblright{} and \textbf{\ru{с}-}, \textquotedblleft{}with.\textquotedblright{}) Is it a true cousin of English \emph{meet}, or only a resemblance in meaning? (\textbf{Only in meaning} — no secure shared root.) How many of this chapter's words so far have no confirmed English cousin so far? (\textbf{Two}: \emph{\ru{скорого}} and \emph{\ru{встречи}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[spakóynay nóchi]{\ru{спокойной} \ru{ночи} — \textquotedblleft{}good night,\textquotedblright{} the chapter's most secure cousin}

\label{lesson:RU-C11-spokoynoy-nochi}



\begin{quote}
The last of six ways to close a conversation — and, fittingly for the final word before sleep, the phrase with the deepest and most secure roots in the whole chapter.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — \ru{спокойной} \ru{ночи}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ru{спокойной} \ru{ночи}} — \emph{spakóynay nóchi} — \textbf{good night}
\end{quote}

Unlike this chapter's five \emph{\ru{до}}-phrases, there is no \emph{\ru{до}} here at all: this is the genitive standing alone, after an unspoken wish — \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}{[}I wish you{]} a calm night.\textquotedblright{}} Say it \emph{spa-KOY-nay NO-chi}. It closes the day the way \emph{\ru{здравствуйте}} opens one, back at the very start of this book: a whole sentence's worth of meaning compressed into two words.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ru{ночь}}, \textquotedblleft{}night,\textquotedblright{} is Proto-Indo-European \textbf{*nók\textsuperscript{w}ts} — one of the most secure cognate sets that survives anywhere in the family, changed almost nothing on its way here: English \textbf{night}, Latin \textbf{nox / noctis} ($\to$ \emph{nocturnal}, \emph{equinox}), Greek \textbf{nýx} ($\to$ \emph{nyctophobia}). Say \emph{\ru{ночь}, night, nox, nyx} together and there is no gap left to explain.

\textbf{\ru{Спокойной}} carries an equally solid, if less obvious, root. It is built on \textbf{\ru{покой}}, \textquotedblleft{}calm, rest, peace,\textquotedblright{} from PIE \textbf{*k\textsuperscript{w}eih\textsubscript{1}-}, \textquotedblleft{}to rest, be quiet\textquotedblright{} — the same root, through Latin \textbf{quiēs}, as English \textbf{quiet}, \textbf{quiescent}, and \textbf{tranquil}; and, through a separate Germanic path (Gothic \emph{hveila}, \textquotedblleft{}a space of time\textquotedblright{}), the same root as English \textbf{while}. Rest, quiet, and \textquotedblleft{}a while\textquotedblright{} all sit on one ancient idea of stillness — and Russian says good night by wishing you both the darkness and the calm in the same two words.

That makes the chapter's tally, word by word: \emph{\ru{свидания}} (cousin: \emph{see}), \emph{\ru{пока}}'s root (cousin: \emph{who/what/why}), \emph{\ru{скорого}} (no cousin), \emph{\ru{завтра}} (cousin: \emph{east}), \emph{\ru{встречи}} (no cousin), and \emph{\ru{ночи}} / \emph{\ru{спокойной}} (\textbf{several cousins each}). The book's last word before sleep turns out to be its best evidence yet that English and Russian are the same language, worn down two very different ways for four thousand years.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\ru{спокойной} \ru{ночи}\textquotedblright{} — \emph{spa-KOY-nay NO-chi}, good night
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\ru{ночь}, night, nox, nyx\textquotedblright{} — one root, barely worn down
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\ru{покой}, quiet, tranquil, while\textquotedblright{} — one more
  \item all six parting words, in order — \textquotedblleft{}\ru{до} \ru{свидания}, \ru{пока}, \ru{до} \ru{скорого}, \ru{до} \ru{завтра}, \ru{до} \ru{встречи}, \ru{спокойной} \ru{ночи}\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}good night.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{\ru{Спокойной} \ru{ночи}}.) Name three English cousins of \emph{\ru{ночь}}. (\textbf{Night, nox, nyx.}) Name two English cousins of \emph{\ru{покой}}. (\textbf{Quiet} and \textbf{tranquil} — or \textbf{while}.) Now reach all the way back to the water-coffee-tea-bread words: what sound does \textbf{\ru{ф}} make, and what does \textbf{\ru{х}} sound like? (\textbf{F}, from \emph{\ru{кофе}}; a raspy \textbf{kh}, from \emph{\ru{хлеб}}.) Ask for tea or bread politely, the pattern \emph{\ru{чай}, \ru{пожалуйста}} already taught. (\textbf{\ru{Чай}, \ru{пожалуйста}. \ru{Хлеб}, \ru{пожалуйста}.})
\end{tcolorbox}
